newsitem.title: USA: New Columbia/HCA CEO to take game plan to government.
newsitem.headline: New Columbia/HCA CEO to take game plan to government.

text.p: The new chief executive of Columbia/HCA Healthcare Corp. said Tuesday that he will devise a plan for changing the company, which is being investigated for fraud, then ask the government for time to implement it.
In an interview, Dr. Thomas Frist said he hopes to bring an end to the sweeping federal investigation of the nation's largest for-profit hospital chain "much quicker than one, two years."

"My goal is to get in here, assess the landscape as quick as possible, come up with a really carefully thought-out, meaningful action plan, present it to them ... ask for further comments or suggestions from them, ask for 90 to 100 days to fully implement that plan and gain their confidence," he said.
A patrician Southerner with a long history in the health are business, Frist, 58, on Friday was named chairman and CEO of the Nashville, Tenn.-based company.

Frist, who had been vice chairman, replaced long-time CEO Richard Scott, who resigned, along with president and chief operating officer David Vandewater, under the cloud of the investigation, which is targeting alleged laboratory billing, home health care and Medicare-related abuses.

In the interview, Frist said he was serious about questions concerning Columbia's practice of offering equity interests in certain company-owned hospitals to physicians that refer patients to those hospitals.
The company recently brought in additional counsel for advice on the issue and moved to halt such physician syndication deals and unwind some of them, Frist said.
The company is also halting an aggressive and costly national advertising campaign started under Scott, Frist said.
"We ought to go back to our roots and have the message delivered for a particular community about the assets of that hospital and build that image up," he said.
Frist said he was part way through interviewing Columbia's six group presidents. He said the talks would help him know who can best take the company forward.
Some of those would come from inside the company, but others would come from outside, he said.
"I should fall back on a few, one or two, key people external to the company who have been tried and proven with me in the past. It's important to have some new faces," he said.

He declined to discuss rumours that Columbia has been in, or has put on hold, merger talks with Santa Barbara, Calif.-based Tenet Healthcare Corp., the second-largest for-profit U.S. hospital company.
He said the company was focused on dealing with the government probe, improving patient care and making internal changes so that Columbia can "have our growth through internal growth for a while."
That said, he added, "As a publicly held company, if somebody approaches us, we must consider it."
Columbia has seen no sign of a slowdown in business due to the government investigation, he said.
"This company is still exceeding overall industry trends," he said, adding that company polls of patient, employee and physician satisfaction have shown no negative trends.
Columbia is scheduled to report second-quarter results Wednesday. Its stock rose 44 cents to $34.56 in consolidated trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
